items.title: Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).
items.summary:
Last week, The Paris Review announced the winners of its annual literary awards. In 2027, Australian author Helen Garner will be feted with the Hadada, a prize that recognizes a writer’s lifelong literary contributions. I am here as an independent body to hype this choice.

Garner—a novelist, journalist, and diarist—writes big-hearted heroines who are often on the edge of a crisis. Her other fans include Lauren Groff, Lily King, Rumaan Alam, and Ben Lerner, but we are legion. Why, you ask?

In a recent piece for The Guardian , Emma Brockes also praised Garner’s “ability to combine insight and erudition of the highest literary order with a style that is at times comically down to earth.” And it’s true—that earthiness is what makes her work indelible. But it’s also just the tip of an iceberg.

Here are three of Garner’s best known books (and why you should make like the Parisians and pick them up, stat).

Monkey Grip , Garner’s 1977 debut, sent a shockwave through Australia. This novel chronicles a woman’s doomed-from-the-jump situationship with a heroin addict who charms her intermittently as they orbit a communal living situation.

A little like Susie Boyt’s sleeper hit, Loved and Missed , this book beautifully captures the recurring heartbreak involved in loving an addict. But it’s never saccharine, or sanctimonious.

Following a bohemian Melbourne milieu that echoes the author’s own set at the time, Garner’s non-judgmental portrait of freewheeling radicals brought out the moralizers on publication. Nora, our heroine, ruffled feathers for depicting ambivalent parenthood…
items.t: Why you should be reading Helen Garner (and where to start).

items.title: Here’s the shortlist for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize.
items.summary:
Today, the Booker Prize Foundation announced the “Great Eight” shortlist of titles for inaugural Children’s Booker Prize, which will be awarded annually beginning in 2027. The Children’s Booker is the latest off-shoot of the prestigious Booker Prize (most recently awarded to M. John Harrison’s The End of Everything ) and celebrates fiction for eight- to 12-year-olds, written in or translated into English and published in the UK or Ireland. The winner will take home £50,000 and the Booker Foundation will be donating at least 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books to children across the United Kingdom and Ireland.

“Any of these books stands comparison with any adult book, whatever the category, on its own terms,” said Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Chair of the Children’s Booker Prize 2027 judges, in the shortlist announcement. He, along with fellow judges Sanchita Basu De Sarkar and Lolly Adefope, narrowed down the shortlist from 89 submissions and will be joined for the final decision by four young people: Ibrahim (12), Lainey (12), Luna (8), and Myla (11).

Here’s the shortlist:

Guy Bass, illustrated by David Roberts, The Worst Thing That Could Possibly Happen 

Catherine Bruton, Tadpole Summer 

Eoin Colfer and Andrew Donkin, illustrated by Giovanni Rigano, War 

Iqbal Hussain, The Night I Borrowed Time 

Liz Hyder, illustrated by Tom de Freston, The Teller of Tall Tales 

Mikey Please, The Rambler’s Curse 

Jessica Scott-Whyte, illustrated by Becka Moor, Séamus Almost Famous 

Shaun Tan, Hometown 

The winner will be announced in a ceremony on February 2, 2027.
items.t: Here’s the shortlist for the first-ever Children’s Booker Prize.

items.title: PEN Writes US Emerges as Free Speech Group “For Writers, by Writers”
items.summary:
Big names in literature are attached to an aspiring PEN Center that launched this week. Omar El Akkad, Ta-Nehisi Coates, Carmen Maria Machado, Sarah McNally, and Percival Everett are among the heavyweights listed as founding members of PEN Writes Us . More than 100 writers, artists, translators, and more are attached to the free speech group.

Pulitzer Prize-winning author and founding member M. Gessen said in a press release announcing the launch:

“I have watched, in more than one country, how the space for speech closes: not all at once, but one exception at a time – one category of speech declared too dangerous, one publisher persuaded to stay quiet. A PEN center’s job is to refuse the exceptions. The United States needs a center that will defend protected speech without carve-outs for whatever is politically inconvenient this year.”

A former PEN America president is among the founding members. Author Dinaw Mengestu resigned as president after the organization released a report about cultural boycotts and the “rising isolation and exclusion” of Israeli and Jewish writers.

PEN Writes US is “dedicated to defending free expression, supporting writers and artists at risk, and championing reading, translation and literature.” The group will seek to join more than 140 PEN centers at the PEN International Congress in September 2027.
items.t: PEN Writes US Emerges as Free Speech Group “For Writers, by Writers”

items.title: Voting Begins for the Final Round of the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards
items.summary:
The opening round of the 2026 Goodreads Choice Awards started November 10th and ended November 22nd. Now, the final round of voting has begun, and it runs until November 29th. The winners are announced December 3rd.

There are books in 15 categories to vote for: Fiction, Historical Fiction, Mystery & Thriller, Romance, Romantasy, Fantasy, Science Fiction, Horror, Debut Novel, Audiobook, Young Adult Fantasy & Sci-Fi, Young Adult Fiction, Nonfiction, Memoir, and History & Biography. These categories are unchanged from last year.

The Goodreads Choice Awards offer the most blatant popularity contest of all the year-end awards: you don’t need to have read all the books in a category to vote for the “best” one. In fact, you don’t even need to have read the book you’re voting for. That introduces a host of problems , and that’s before getting into the fact that Amazon owns Goodreads. Still, it makes for a good snapshot of the books getting the most attention at this point in time.

You can vote on the Goodreads website .

Keep up with all the latest book news by signing up for the Book Riot Newsletter .

items.title: The New York Times Shares Their 100 Notable Books of 2026
items.summary:
‘Tis the season for Best Books of the Year lists, from Barnes & Noble’s overall #1 pick to the sprawling 389-book list from NPR . The New York Times list falls somewhere in the middle, with 100 fiction and nonfiction books selected by NYT staff.

As you might expect, there are a lot of literary fiction books represented, like American Hagwon by Min Jin Lee, The Disappearers by Marlon James, and Canon by Paige Lewis. But plenty of other genres make an appearance, including romance ( Star Shipped by Cat Sebastian), horror ( Off the Reservation by Stephen Graham Jones), science fiction ( Earth 7 by Deb Olin Unferth), and cultural history ( Darkology by Rhae Lynn Barnes).

You’ll find familiar titles here, like the bestselling Yesteryear by Caro Claire Burke and Strangers by Belle Burden, as well as the Booker Prize-winning The End of Everything by M. John Harris. There are also books that have been on many of the other best books of the year lists, like John of John by Douglas Stuart.

Mixed in are some more obscure picks, including Korean Messiah by Jonathan Cheng, The Radiance by Ayad Akhtar, and It Will Come Back to You by Sigrid Nunez.

You can find the full list at The New York Times . They also offer a cheat sheet for selecting your first read off the list. 

Keep up with all the latest book news by signing up for the Book Riot Newsletter .

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Novels of 2026
items.summary:
It’s been, in my opinion, an excellent year for novels. So excellent that this list was exceedingly hard to whittle down. We had long-awaited books from beloved authors like Marlon James, Min Jin Lee, and Ben Lerner—occupying vastly opposite ends of the page-count spectrum—and countless exciting debuts. But what’s thrilled me most about all the books I’ve read this year is how strange, distinct, and utterly human they are. 

I’ve expounded before on the value of literature in the age of AI, but we are another year deeper into its all-too-rapid encroachment on our art, so you’ll have to forgive me for getting up on my soapbox once again. As em-dashes are being described as a hallmark of AI-writing rather than as a writer’s favorite punctuation mark to overuse, now co-opted by the machines who stole from us, I’ve found myself asking: What, exactly, makes art human ? If we are being asked to rethink even our grammar choices so as not to be mistaken for robots, how do we make art that is profoundly and undeniably our own? 

I can’t say whether or not the authors on this list were writing with this question in mind, but I can say for certain that for me, their books are answering it. Our favorite books of 2026 got weird , in every sense of the word. They got creative on a line-level, on a structure-level, on a content-level. They are utterly distinct in their voice and style, from Scott McClanahan’s Fights! to the numerous narrators of The Disappearers , each instantly identifiable by voice. Some grapple with existential questions about our technological age more directly: Ben…

items.title: The Comics Library Commons Connects Libraries with Indie Comics
items.summary:
Jack Phoenix is a comics lover and librarian. He’s here with a piece about a project he’s been working on to make discovery and access to independent comics easier for librarians eager, the Comics Library Commons. 

***

As most folks who work in libraries know, comics–including graphic novels, and manga–are often the most circulated and popular books on the library shelves. For those librarians who specialize in comics, two questions constantly come up. From fellow librarians it’s “How do I find the really good independent comics for our library?”. From independent comics creators it’s “How do I get my books onto library shelves?”

Sadly, there has not been a good answer to either one until now.

The Comics Library Commons (CLC), a nonprofit, online resource where libraries can shop for independent comics, graphic novels, and zines not available through the typical library vendors, is coming early 2027. CLC will provide a variety of resources, including reviews, best practices, MARC records, a newsletter, and more, all of which will be vetted by a degreed librarian. What’s more, the money from any books purchased through CLC will go directly to the indie creator or indie publisher.

Here is how it will work: a library selector will hop onto CLC’s website. When they find a book they want, they purchase it using a library credit card or through a process of invoicing, purchase order, and issuing a check.

This payment goes directly to the creator, with CLC taking a minimal, prearranged cut. The comic creator will also have the option of keeping 100% of the payment and pay…
items.t: The Comics Library Commons Connects Libraries with Indie Comics

items.title: 8 Sapphic Gothic Novels to Haunt Your Shelves
items.summary:
One of my favorite subgenres is sapphic gothic novels. Gothics are already queer-coded: Rebecca by Daphne du Maurier is infamous for its lesbian subtext, and no one can convince me that Theo in The Haunting of Hill House by Shirley Jackson is a straight woman. But lately, we’ve gotten an influx of sapphic gothic novels where the queer content goes beyond subtext. These all have sapphic main characters, though not necessarily a sapphic romance—if you’re going into a gothic novel expecting a Happily Ever After, you’re in the wrong place!

This is far from a complete list: dozens of sapphic gothic novels have been released by mainstream publishers in the past handful of years. These eight are a great place to start.

House of Beth by Kerry Cullen 
 Cassie is starting over after a devastating breakup with her girlfriend and a breakdown at her job. She returns to her hometown, where she bumps into her high school friend, Eli, who is now a widower with two kids. Only a few months later, she’s married to him and homeschooling his kids in the woods. But nothing she does lives up to the image of Eli’s first wife, Beth. (Sound familiar ?) She’s also struggling with harm OCD, and violent images invade her mind. Cassie begins to hear the house speak to her, telling her the secrets of what really happened to Eli’s first wife.

Although Cassie hasn’t repressed her queerness, I see this as a story about compulsory heterosexuality. Cassie is trying to become the perfect wife and (step)mother and failing—she begins to crumble under the pressure of not meeting these standards. She has fled…

items.title: Quick Holiday Tips for Science Fiction and Fantasy Readers
items.summary:
You would think the science fiction and fantasy readers could fly off to other worlds while dealing with flight delays or family dysfunction. But even we need help when confronting the particularities of holiday travel. The logistics and events of the fall and winter season may be harrowing, heartwarming, enraging, anticipatory, or all of the above. It makes sense that Planes, Trains, and Automobiles is the quintessential movie to brace ourselves for the holiday season. These books and holiday travel tips for science fiction and fantasy readers are intended to similarly ready us for the chaos.

Immerse Yourself in a Full Cast Audiobook 

Whether you’re staring down a long flight or stuck in an airport for hours, immersive entertainment is your friend. If you need a break from screens but not from epic storytelling, download a well-reviewed full-cast audiobook or two ahead of your trip. World War Z: The Complete Edition, An Oral History of the Zombie War by Max Brooks or Black Sun by Rebecca Roanhorse are both popular, well-reviewed full cast productions if you’re looking for a starting place.

Avoid Harrowing Interstellar Thrillers 

While facing down your fears through fiction can be cathartic, might I recommend skipping that method if your holiday plans involve flying. The holidays are stressful enough without elevated cortisol from space travel murder and mayhem a la The Deep Sky by Yume Kitasei or deeply triggering first contact stories like The Sparrow by Mary Doria Russell. Both of these books are engrossing reads that will still be there after your safe travels.…
items.t: Quick Holiday Tips for Science Fiction and Fantasy Readers

items.title: 3 Books to Read for Indigenous Heritage Month
items.summary:
Aaron John Curtis is the author of the debut novel Old School Indian , out now in paperback from Tin House/Zando. Below, he recommends three books to read for Indigenous Heritage Month. (Photo credit: CacáSantoro. )

Project 562: Changing the Way We See Native America by Matika Wilbur (Swinomish and Tulalip) 
 The most important book to come out of Indian Country in decades because it places us—all of us—firmly in the present moment. There are more than 562 federally recognized tribes (575 as I type) and hundreds of unrecognized tribes, but 562 is how many there were when Matika Wilber set out on what would become a 10-year project to document someone from each Native nation in the US. This is Medicine with a capital M, but on a practical level, if you’ve ever had a silly question you were too embarrassed to ask your Native friend, you’ll find the answer here. As a bonus, it’ll look amazing on your coffee table and makes a great gift.

The Buffalo Hunter Hunter by Stephen Graham Jones (Blackfeet) 
 No other book I’ve read, in fiction or nonfiction, holds up a mirror to U.S. history the way this book does. Partially it’s the meticulous research of the Marias Massacre and decimation of the American buffalo, but mostly it’s because our protagonist, Good Stab, is a vampire who’s lived through it all. History will never feel so alive to the reader as in these undead pages.

A disturbing account of the way Russia’s elites have reduced themselves to craven courtiers

When Vladimir Putin launched his full-scale invasion of Ukraine four and a half years ago, it was a shock, but it wasn’t a surprise. The US and the UK had been publicly warning their allies for weeks about what Russia was planning, as well as threatening the Russians with a wave of sanctions unprecedented against a major power.

Putin’s foreign policy had long relied on confusion and untruth. By saying that they knew exactly what he was up to, Britain and America were hoping first to deny him his usual ambiguity, and second to pressure the men around him into making him stop, since war would deprive them of the stolen assets they’d stashed in London’s most exclusive neighbourhoods.

items.title: When A Farewell to Arms Was Censored For Foul Language
items.summary:
The young novelist Ernest Hemingway was angry and frustrated. Scribner’s Magazine had decided to cut “shit,” “fuck,” “balls,” “cocksucker,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” and “Jesus Christ” from his new book, A Farewell to Arms , when it began serializing it in May 1929. The semi-autobiographical novel followed the experiences of an American ambulance driver on the Italian Front in World War I. For publication as a book, Maxwell Perkins, Hemingway’s editor at Charles Scribner’s Sons, managed to get the last three phrases restored, in sentences such as “I shot the son of a bitch with my rifle,” “they were loading the girls from the soldiers’ whorehouse into a truck,” and “Jesus Christ what I could do with two hundred and fifty dollars.” Hemingway and Perkins negotiated, the editor conceding “scrotum” instead of “balls,” but refusing “c—s r” as an alternative to “cocksucker” (which became, instead, “‘I killed that –  of a sergeant’ ”). The author had to turn his other “four-letter words” into phrases like “Go something yourself.” Hemingway protested that “emasculation was a minor operation to perform on men, animals, and books, but its effect was great.” He was waging a fight for “full use of the language.” But he gave in.

Hemingway had won part of his fight. But predictably, “scrotum,” “son of a bitch,” “whore,” “Jesus Christ” (as an exclamation), and the premarital love affair at the novel’s core were themselves too much for the Word Police, at least in some jurisdictions. In Boston—a city already known for its gusto in banning any work of literature or art deemed indecent by…

items.title: How Important Were Medieval Viking Drinking Games?
items.summary:
It’s clear from mythology that alcohol was ritually significant in Norse culture, and none more so than mead, which was considered a godly drink and one that imbued the drinker with poetic skill.

In the ancient sagas the origin story of mead comes from a daring series of thefts, with the drink first created through the spit-based peace negotiations of two warring god-families. Their congealing spit, naturally, birthed a mystic with the highest intelligence called Kvasir whose blood was in fact all mead, and through this blood flowed poetry itself.

Unfortunately, Kvasir was not intelligent enough to avoid murder by dwarves for his blood-mead, and then this precious liquid was stolen again by a giant. Odin, king of the gods, wanted his own share of this bloody-mega-mead and so disguised himself as an eagle and stole the mead from the giant, allegedly seducing the giant’s daughter in the process. As Odin escaped from the giant’s lair, some of the mead was spilled from his eagle’s beak and fell to earth. It was said that the great Norse saga poets were those folk who by luck were struck by drops of falling mead from Odin’s beak.

Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty.

*

Beyond the wild and winding escapades of the gods in pursuit of blood-mead, we know a lot of drinking also happened in the mortal Norse realms. Booze was a bind which helped keep Norse society together, with shared drinking a way of professing loyalty and signing contracts, from marriage to inheritance. This drinking, along with most…

items.title: Seven Books That Show What Architecture Tells Us About Storytelling
items.summary:
It was 1976, and as I drove through Marin County, north of San Francisco, an enormous building emerged from the distant hills. It seemed almost otherworldly, as if a spacecraft had landed in a field and burrowed its way into the ground.

It was the Marin County Civic Center, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright.

I was captivated by this strange, futuristic building. Its muted pink structure and long, low profile extended into the valley, while its circular and semicircular openings were classical and serene. The building seemed to belong to the landscape even as it challenged it.

I didn’t have the vocabulary then to explain what I was experiencing. I only knew that a structure had altered my perception of the world around it.

Years later, I understood that my draw towards architecture was the relationship between structure and experience. How does a room hold memory? How does a building establish a sense of place? What happens to a structure when people inhabit it, when their histories become entangled with its own?

These questions are not so different from those a writer might ask. A novel, like a building, has a framework (beginning, middle, and end) that holds its parts together: passages that lead us from one place to another, openings that illuminate or obscure a path. Within this framework, writers use language and syntax as an architect uses a straight-edge and pencil. But the most compelling buildings, like the most compelling stories, are more than the sum of their parts. Something happens when human experience enters the structure of both: they’re altered by memory…
items.t: Seven Books That Show What Architecture Tells Us About Storytelling

items.title: “The Rib Remembers,” a Poem by Awuor Ouma
items.summary:
It was not the mouth that first spoke,

but the bone.

The rib did not ask,

it fractured.

They say she was made from it,

but no one asked what she left behind.

The women in my bloodline

crack like this:

with grace sharp enough

to cut their silence open.

They are not broken,

only reshaped

by what they had to survive.

Grief taught them posture.

Pain taught them to sing.

Their softness was never surrender,

only the veil they wore

while sharpening their names.

_____________________________

From Blue Hands, Brown Skin by Awuor Ouma. Copyright © 2026. Available from University of Georgia Press. Blue Hands, Brown Skin was selected by D.S. Marriott for the Cave Canem Prize.
items.t: “The Rib Remembers,” a Poem by Awuor Ouma

items.title: Kylie Cheung on the Fake Victimhood of Abusers, From Johnny Depp to Israel
items.summary:
In the spring of 2022, Kylie Cheung was reporting for Jezebel on stories she considered urgent; stories about sexual assault and intimate partner violence. In the background, a celebrity defamation trial was being livestreamed on social media. As she watched Johnny Depp’s legal team recast Amber Heard’s resistance to his abuse as proof that she was the abuser, Cheung came to see the trial as a textbook case of DARVO: Deny, Attack, Reverse Victim and Offender—the abuser’s playbook that psychologist Jennifer Freyd named in 1997. 

Playing the Victim: How Empires and Abusers Fake Victimhood to Hold Power—And How We Fight Back (North Atlantic Books) follows that playbook from the intimate to the imperial. Cheung argues that powerful institutions, from the Israeli state to anti-abortion lawmakers to the U.S. immigration system, hold on to power by performing victimhood and casting the people they oppress as the aggressors. Israel’s genocide in Gaza is the book’s central case study. Drawing on interviews with human rights lawyers, humanitarian workers, doctors and sexual violence researchers, Cheung documents the sexual and reproductive violence inflicted on Palestinians and the rape atrocity propaganda used to justify it. 

Cheung and I spoke about how a celebrity trial became a book about empire, what it means to write about a genocide as it unfolds, and what this work costs the people who do it. 

* 

Samaa Khullar: The book opens with your 2022 coverage of Depp v. Heard, and you write that it would fundamentally alter your understanding of power and patriarchy. You also said…
items.t: Kylie Cheung on the Fake Victimhood of Abusers, From Johnny Depp to Israel

items.title: Long Wave
items.summary:
Ruth 

There is the house in the town where Ruth grew up and ran away from. There is the door with the lock and the garden with the tree and the school car park in the darkness. There is the river hurrying out of the town and passing through the country and to the sea. There is Ruth when she was a child and the dream of the island moved up the walls of her room and became almost all she could see. There is, now, Ruth—a decade gone from the house in the town—on the island, finally. There is the island. Here it is. Magnificent and terrifying, divine. It was made so long ago, it was battered by ice from the rock. Here and there, in the craggy cliff, the ground opens up, smaller and larger entrances leading to caves and tunnels below, the gush and bellow of the sea moving in and out. At the highest point, a white exclamation mark: a lighthouse.

Ruth leaves her daughter at the lighthouse and walks out to the cliff. At some point she stops and looks back to see if she can make out the clearing where Ori waits, but already it is out of sight. She keeps going. She sees birds with white-tipped arrow wings, seals slipping into the water. She sees beaches protected from the wind. She must go back now. She must. OK, she says, here I come.

She turns and starts walking back to Ori. The ground is treacherous. The island spins around her, fills her; she keeps walking. As she walks she gives away some of the island—it belongs only to her, beloved, the clear and ringing dream of it that she has had since she was a child in that house by the river—and she thinks: I am walking to Ori. I am…

items.title: The Song of Stork and Dromedary by Anjet Daanje review – don’t miss this glorious epic inspired by Emily Brontë
items.summary:
The afterlife of a Yorkshire village girl who becomes a gothic literary icon is explored across three centuries, in a thrilling paean to the power of books

I had a plan. I was going to nibble away at this great wedge of a book, a morsel a night, like a little reading mouse. But then the story swallowed me whole. I read Dutch author Anjet Daanje’s The Song of Stork and Dromedary over three feverish nights, and spent the days in between longing for the dark. This 720-page novel should come with a warning label: may cause severe infatuation.

We begin in the fictional Yorkshire village of Bridge Fowling with Susan Knowles-Chester, a woman who attends to the dead. The year is 1847, and Susan knows the old ways, the threshold rituals: how to arrange a corpse so it doesn’t gape and gawp at the living. “The villagers have a horror of her work, for wherever she goes, she leaves grief like driftwood in her wake, yet when the time comes, many ask for her help, it is an open secret.”

items.title: More sex, different endings: how fan fiction makes our dreams come true
items.summary:
From Heated Rivalry to Harry Potter, popular series are inspiring fan fiction read by thousands online. Now the authors of those online works are getting publishing deals of their own

Shortly after this year’s London book fair, rumours began to circulate of a seven-figure book deal for the author of the wildly popular work of Harry Potter fan fiction All the Young Dudes. First published between 2017 and 2018 by user MsKingBean89 on the online platform Archive of Our Own, All the Young Dudes is arguably the most-read work of fan fiction of all time. Now its author will write a trilogy under the pen name BN King, with the first novel, Wolfboy, due to be published in autumn 2027.

This is by no means the first example of fan fiction crossing over into mainstream publishing: the bestselling debut of 2025, Alchemised, also started off as fan fiction based on the Harry Potter series, with some inspiration from The Handmaid’s Tale too. And nearly 15 years earlier, EL James published Fifty Shades of Grey, which began life as Twilight fan fiction before proceeding, in its new guise, to sell millions of copies worldwide.

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026
items.summary:
This year, I read more nonfiction books than ever before. It wasn’t planned, though I suppose it had something to do with wanting to understand a world that seems increasingly fractured and confounding. For years, one political crisis has given way to another, each arriving with its own predictions of what terrible thing awaits us next. Reading nonfiction offered a way of making sense of it all, beyond the endless stream of news on my screen.

Curiously, the books that helped me best think about the future were often concerned with the past. In Turn (W)here , Chet’la Sebree reckons with America’s history of racism as she considers what it would mean to raise a Black child in a country still shaped by that history. The past can make the future feel all too predictable. These days, it’s hard not to imagine what’s coming in dystopian terms, from climate catastrophe to forever wars to—new fear unlocked—AI-driven human extinction.

And yet, history has a way of defying our expectations. The recent victories of the political left in this year’s midterm elections felt like a fulcrum—the whole country tilted blue and another future became imaginable. Of course, I am wary of getting carried away by optimism; the past is full of futures that never arrived. In An Army of Lovers Cannot Fail , Hélène Giannecchini recovers forgotten forms of intimacy and solidarity through the stories of queer people whose lives and ways of living have been largely overlooked.

If the past is riddled with unrealized possibilities, perhaps the task is not simply to recover them, but to imagine new ones.…
items.t: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Nonfiction Books of 2026

items.title: Our Son Is Practicing in the Basement for His Interplanetary Voyage
items.summary:
“Mars” by Peter Stamm 

He’s leaving us, going further and further away, by now he’s 118 million kilometers away, the loneliest man in the universe, and with each hour it’s another hundred thousand kilometers. He tried to explain the route to me, how we’re moving and he’s moving in this three-­dimensional system of moving objects, and the stars and planets are moving around each other. The quickest ways are not always the shortest, you use the gravitational pull of an object to catapult yourself faster and further away from it, follow a curved space within a curved space, into infinite distance. Is it even true to say you fly in space, is it not more like being still while everything else around you is in motion?

You have to believe, Laurin said, it’s the only way to survive. I only survive myself by believing. Six months and nineteen days. And then? Then he opens the basement door, and he’s standing on Mars. Laurin calls it a mission; I call it an experiment.

He was months in preparation, getting the equipment and materials together, planning and outfitting the rooms and documenting everything. It’s his baby, he didn’t want any support, and no one apart from the three of us knows about it. Will he go public once he’s reached his objective? He shrugs. That’s not what it’s for. He hates being the focus of attention, the only thing that matters is to prove to his own satisfaction that he can do it.

From the outset, his mother thought the idea was batty. She resisted it; I helped him, marginally. It was the only way not to lose him completely in that time of feverish­…

items.title: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses
items.summary:
The rock critic’s obsessive yet incisive sorting of musical genius is a contrarian delight

As veteran US music journalist Bill Wyman (no relation to the Stones bassist) would be the first to point out, the listicle is not a revered form of internet journalism. It labours under a ghastly portmanteau name that simply jams together “list” and “article” but somehow carries a hint of the diminutive about it, which the listicle’s detractors would say is absolutely right: a chart – a Top 20 or 50 or 100 – with each entry warranting a brief paragraph of explication, they are reviled as a cheap, largely effortless way to fill space online. They are also astoundingly popular, particularly when the subject is music, perhaps because people were compiling rock and pop’s history into listicles decades before the internet came along.

The NME got there first, in 1974, with what it called a “Writers’ All-Time Top 100 Albums” list – a bold early attempt to define a canon of classic rock, with Sgt Pepper at No 1 and black and female artists sorely under­represented. But it wasn’t until the 90s that the idea really grew legs. Suddenly the music press was awash with retrospective charts, evidence that an increasingly rosy view of rock history was abroad: the 90s also saw the rise of the heritage rock magazine, the expensively packaged retrospective box set and, indeed, of Britpop, an entire genre more or less predicated on evoking vague memories of the past, as if something of its magic might rub off through imitation.
items.t: Bill Wyman’s Rock & Roll Lists review – greatest hits and biggest misses

items.title: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Short Story Collections of 2026
items.summary:
It’s been a particularly fruitful year for the short story. In Recommended Reading alone, we’ve had the honor of publishing excerpts from many of our favorite collections of the year. Along with surprising variance and singularity, there are also recurrences across these collections: identity, artifice, and distance—both temporal and physical—mediate the relationships at the core of these books.

In her introduction to Lim Sunwoo’s story “That Unfamiliar Night,” translator Chi-Young Kim writes: “Lim beautifully portrays how grounding it can be when someone sees you, when someone is quietly there for you.” Across these collections, a reader has this sense of bearing witness—and being seen—by so many small moments. In Bret Anthony Johnston’s “Paradeability” , a father accompanies his son to a clown convention in Texas; the costumes and air of performance both amplify and conceal vulnerability. In Sydney Rende’s “Monsters” , the dissolution of a relationship is distorted in the funhouse mirror of reality TV. In “Going Up” from Chris Vanjonack’s Out of Body , an anonymous speaker targets a woman plagued by uncertainty. Above all, our favorite collections this year play with ambiguity: What can be revealed when a story withholds a tidy answer to its central questions? 

This year’s best works of short stories include five debut collections, as well as new collections from veterans of the form, such as Bret Anthony Johnston and Emily Ruskovich. Regardless of where you start, there are many delights to be found above—and below—the surface of these narratives.
–Lennie…
items.t: Electric Lit’s Top 10 Short Story Collections of 2026

items.title: A Night at the 77th National Book Awards
items.summary:
The National Book Awards is arguably the year’s biggest night in books. It’s glam (Black-tie! Tuxedos! Champagne!), it’s fun (think cocktails on the dance floor next to literary all-stars), and, at its best, it’s political. It’s a moment for writers to take the stage and speak out against global injustice and the injustices we are facing from within our own industry. Last night’s ceremony was all of the above, and I got to experience it live, reporting the event with former Electric Lit intern Amulya Tadimety, who graciously helped me record the evening. (Shout out to Amulya, who even swapped phones with me so I could write down quotes while she took pictures using the higher-quality camera.)

This year featured a phenomenal set of finalists in all categories, many of whom Electric Lit is lucky to have featured in our digital pages. In Fiction, we featured an interview with Valeria Luiselli and a joint conversation with Morgan Thomas and Julián Delgado Lopera , the two trans novelists nominated for the award—an exciting and much-deserved first that I hope marks many more to come. In Nonfiction, we published interviews with Abdelrahman ElGendy , Sara Nović , and Camonghne Felix , as well as a reading list from Joseph Osmundson , who also helped us put together an article about Bret Stephens’ hideous New York Times hit piece about the diversity of the year’s longlist.

The event was hosted by Kyle MacLachlan, whose opening remarks set the tone for the night: at times, lighthearted, balanced with appropriate seriousness. He gave a much appreciated nod to library cards and…

items.title: A Call to Action from Electric Literature
items.summary:
Dear Reader,

Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was a blatant attack on trans people, period—and applying would have been a betrayal of the values held so closely by EL and its community. I was part of the decision to forgo funding, and while it was nerve-wracking to walk away from money we relied on, standing up for our beliefs was a no-brainer. We trusted that our community would have our back and fill the gap. And it did.

When I was preparing to take over as Executive Director and Publisher earlier this year, EL had the chance to speak publicly (in an amicus brief attached to a lawsuit targeting the NEA) about how the loss of NEA funding impacted our ability to practice free speech as an independent literary magazine. As I was interviewed by lawyers from the National Coalition Against Censorship, I took a moment to reflect on the prior year. I felt more sure of our decision than ever. Though our funding had been cut, though we had been forced to revise our financial strategy without notice, we stood with the communities whose rights, protection, and humanity we are forever committed to uplifting—trans people and the queer community, people of color, people with disability, immigrants, women. Rather than feeling fearful about what the future might hold, I only felt immense…
